title: UPDATE: Cybersecurity Stocks Gain 10% to 15% as AI Slowdown Calls Hit Chipmakers
summary:
Cybersecurity shares rose 10% to 15% while semiconductor stocks fell about 5% on Sept. 14, as calls by Anthropic and OpenAI to slow AI development raised concerns about demand for computing infrastructure. The rally extended across software, with a median gain of 4.5% among companies tracked by Tomasz Tunguz. Of the 87 stocks in his index, 80 advanced and 12 gained at least 10%.

Nvidia fell 2.8% and Oracle declined 4.3%. Earlier, SoftBank closed down 11% in Japan, and its US depositary receipts dropped 12.5% before the US market opened. CoreWeave fell 9% in premarket trading, while Nasdaq futures lost 1.6%. The infrastructure selloff reflected concerns that slower development of advanced models could reduce demand for GPUs, memory, networking and data centers.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged slower capability improvements over the weekend so safety work could keep up, winning support from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Anthropic and OpenAI committed to giving independent evaluators access comparable to employees to assess their systems. Amodei said the proposal did not mean halting training or technical progress. Asked on CBS whether Anthropic would stop releasing more advanced models, he said: “It doesn't mean that. What it means is that we need to make sure that every generation of models that we release is properly tested.”

FT: AI stocks slid as frontier labs turned safety concerns into a possible spending slowdown.

Over the weekend, top labs (OpenAI/Anthropic) explicitly argued that labs should slow model capability improvements so risk prevention can catch up.

Investors are translating that safety discipline into a spending question because slower frontier training can reduce near-term demand for GPUs, memory, networking, and data centers.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Dario Amodei got personal on CBS about AI’s risks, benefits, and the ridicule he faces on social media over safety.

"I feel that this is a technology with great benefits and great risks. 

My father died of a disease, hepatitis C, that was something like 40% curable when he died of it. He wasn't one of the ones who was cured. A few years after, a medicine was invented that made it 95% curable.

I myself survived an early-stage cancer that, if I'd been living in 1950, I probably would have died from. So I feel the weight of bringing the benefits of this technology.

I also feel the risks. I wake up every day and, you know, I read one of these threat reports, like someone tried to use our model to build biological weapons. Of course, I don't want to be responsible for that, and that's why we have very strong safeguards.

Almost every day, I'm made fun of on social media because our model's biology safeguards are too strong. Biology students complain, and they make jokes that they can't use the model. But the reason for that is that we have strong safeguards.

I would rather they make fun of me than wake up one day and discover that someone used our model, Claude, to kill a bunch of people. I don't want that.

So I feel both sides of it. I feel both sides of the responsibility."

----
From "CBS Sunday Morning" YouTube channel, (full video link in comment)

We Must Pace the Frontier: I’ve written a new essay on why the AI industry should slow down, with a three-part plan for doing so.

Anthropic is unilaterally committing to the first of these steps. We’ll provide third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training.

selectedTweets.text:
Another strong statement from Sam Altman on slowing down AI.

“Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.” https://t.co/cb2PlJ34dF
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.
